front.title: To Pray Is to Wander
front.note: A record of light. A record of the strangeness of being alive.

appears.description: To Pray Is to Wander About the Meaning of Life. A record of light. A record of the strangeness of being alive. Photographs and writing by Habib Saleh, made in Lebanon.

pages.title: Prelude
paras: There are moments when the world seems to withdraw from its own noise, and something quietly begins to appear. Nothing extraordinary has happened. The streets remain the same, light still falls across familiar walls, children continue to play, seasons return as they always have. And yet, the ordinary begins to resist its own familiarity.

What follows is an ongoing body of work unfolding through photography, writing, and film. These are not separate practices or independent projects, but different ways of approaching the same experience. Each movement, each photographic story, and each fragment belongs to a longer wandering through the ordinary mysteries of being alive.

This work does not move toward conclusions. It lingers with places, people, gestures, and passing moments, allowing them to reveal themselves without asking them to become symbols or explanations. Some parts speak through images, others through words. Neither is complete on its own. Together, they move toward what neither can fully hold.
The pages that follow are not meant to be hurried through. They are invitations to look a little longer, to remain with what is already here before familiarity quietly covers it again.

pages.title: Colored
pages.note: Colored Air was the first name I gave to a change I did not yet understand.

pieces.label: Ojibwe proverb
pieces.text: Sometimes I go about in pity for myself, and all the while, a great wind carries me across the sky.

Colored Air was the first name I gave to a change I did not yet understand.

The world itself had not become different, but my relationship to it had. Familiar places began to feel strangely vivid. The ordinary resisted its own familiarity. Children playing in the street, an old man sitting outside his home, flowers returning with the seasons, evening light moving across a familiar wall, nothing extraordinary had happened, yet everything seemed quietly charged with a presence I had spent years overlooking.

The title came before I understood what it meant. It described a feeling more than an idea, as though even the air itself had become saturated with something I had not noticed before.

These photographs were made among the people and places closest to me, my family, my village, the cities I move through, and the ordinary rhythms that shape them. They are not attempts to preserve these moments against time, nor to transform them into symbols. They are traces of encounters, brief moments in which the world quietly revealed itself before returning once again to the ordinary.

I photograph because the photograph is the most immediate expression of something I have seen and felt. It begins before thought has organized the encounter. The camera does not teach me to look, it follows a way of seeing that is already there.

Color is more than appearance. It carries the inner atmosphere of the moment, not only what the camera recorded, but what being there felt like.

No matter how vivid the colors of poetry, or how carefully one chooses their words, description always falls short of the true essence of reality. However rich the imagination, it can never come close to the raw, sometimes absurd intensity of what actually exists.

pieces.label: The Season of the Mulberry, 2025
pieces.text:
In the village of Joun, the first mulberries of the season are ready.

My father’s uncle Khalil, a quiet man of the land, gardener to others and farmer for himself, asked me to come along. He wanted me to taste the first berries from two trees he had been tending. I often follow him on these small, unhurried walks. There is something about the way he moves through gardens, as though time itself slows down.

I brought my camera with me.

pieces.label: When Roses Bloom, 2025
pieces.text:
Photographs from the days I spent with my father’s uncle Anis.

Each evening, he moved quietly among the rose bushes he had tended for years, gathering the flowers one by one as the last light settled over the garden.

I followed with my camera, drawn to the calm in his gestures and to the silence that arrives with the fading light.

A gesture repeated so many times it has become invisible. A door that still opens. The way the light falls in a particular room at a particular hour as if it has been practicing for years.

These are not symbols. They are not evidence of anything. They are just what is here, what keeps being here.

There are days the light is more than I can take, and I wait them out in a dark room.

Sorrow does this. It moves through a place the way weather moves through a place, changing what it touches without destroying it. What remains after is not what was there before, but it is not nothing either. It is something else, something that has been through the full weight of what happened and did not empty out.
Ordinary and ordinary and ordinary until it breaks your heart.

Nothing is simply okay or not okay. People move through life trying to understand what any of it means without ever fully arriving at an answer.

For some of us, experience arrives layered and intense, carrying more weight than it seems to for others. Connection is not always easy. Belonging can feel distant, and that distance often leaves a quiet void.

Still, there is value in understanding oneself, and in allowing the inner world the space and rest it needs to breathe. Loneliness and boredom are not necessarily things to fear. Belonging is not always a condition for meaning.

Constant activity can be an illusion of productivity, and movement is often mistaken for purpose. At times, thinking is needed more than acting.

The self is restless and hungry for attention, from itself and from others, always circling its own echo. Yet standing still can be a way of seeing more clearly.

Sometimes what is required is not participation but observation, because lingering over a problem too forcefully often amplifies it instead of resolving it.

This chapter emerged after a period of personal loss that permanently altered my way of seeing. Yet over time the work moved beyond the event that initiated it. What remained was something simpler, and perhaps more difficult to describe: an increasing attentiveness to the quiet persistence of life itself.

Looking gradually ceased to feel like searching. It became a way of remaining available.

pages.title: What Light Knows
pages.note: I return to one photograph constantly.

pieces.text:
I return to one photograph constantly.

It shows a birthday table with a white cake my mother prepared, topped with a few candles leaning toward one side. Around it, members of my family gather, some smiling, others frozen in incomplete movements. If I shake the photograph gently, the moment itself seems to move. I turn the page and return. The colours have faded, and the album grows heavier in my hands. That was my first lesson that things pass.

I wasn’t always drawn to the photographs themselves, but to the way they existed within our home. Some belonged to weddings or birthdays. Others were gathered only because they were taken in the same year. Then there were the photographs that never found their place at all, loose images left inside envelopes, preserving ordinary afternoons, passing gestures, unfinished moments, things too quiet to belong anywhere except memory.

Our house in the village of Joun changed over the years. Rooms were added, walls rebuilt, windows opened, yet many spaces never lost the names of those who had once lived within them. My grandmother’s room is still called Hajje Fatima’s room, although she has long been gone. The room became something else. The name never did.

The elderly still move through the village using names that no longer belong to what stands before them. Perhaps they are not forgetting. Perhaps they continue to inhabit another layer of the same place. Sometimes I think photography does something similar. It allows different moments to remain together without asking them to become one.

After returning to Joun, I found myself photographing passing light, moving bodies, familiar rooms, gardens, and the slow changes that rarely announce themselves. I wasn’t searching for the past. I was trying to remain close to what was quietly becoming memory while it was still here.

One begins to think of truth only in the midst of searching. When the search subsides, even the word loses weight, leaving a space where questions no longer press.

Words lean toward it but never quite arrive. A sentence begins to point, yet by its ending, something has already slipped away.

Pages gather into books, yet when they close, the matter feels unfinished.

Thoughts reach outward, but their grasp leaves only an outline, never the shape itself.

Truth moves just beyond expression, near enough to sense, too wide to contain, hovering where language falters, where thought grows quiet, where searching itself comes to rest.

Perhaps it is not found in definition, but in what escapes it; not in the structure of belief, but in the loosening of belief.

Perhaps, in the end, what remains of truth is a feeling.

Perhaps this is what light has always known about us. It falls on everything equally, without choosing between what is arriving and what is leaving. It witnesses change without trying to preserve it. The photographs that follow are not an attempt to stop time, but to remain present as it passes.

pages.title: Before It
pages.note: There comes a moment when a place no longer belongs only to the present. It begins to exist in two times at once, as something still lived, and something already becoming memory.

pieces.text:
There comes a moment when a place no longer belongs only to the present. It begins to exist in two times at once, as something still lived, and something already becoming memory.

Before It Disappears follows this quiet transformation through my village of Joun, where I returned after years of living in Beirut. It is less concerned with disappearance itself than with the strange experience of witnessing it while life continues. Children still play in the streets, flowers return with the seasons, families gather, old men sit outside their homes. Nothing has stopped. And yet something has already begun to slip away.

Over the years, wars, migration, economic collapse, and the slow movement of time have altered the village and the lives around it. Houses empty, generations leave, familiar rhythms become quieter. What changes is not only the place itself, but the way it is inhabited, remembered, and carried by those who remain.

These photographs do not attempt to preserve the village against time or to mourn it before it is gone. They remain close to what is still here, attentive to the fragile coexistence of presence and disappearance. They ask what it means to love a place while knowing it cannot remain as it is.

Places survive within us after they have changed. People remain after they have gone.

There are moments when time slips and what was once returns to you so vividly, with such detail, that it unsettles you. Was it ever real, or only a dream? The question is not the point. The point is the returning, the fact that something in you still receives it, still trembles at it, still opens when every logic says to close.
Beauty and difficulty do not resolve one another. Innocence and violence, tenderness and destruction, play and seriousness can appear within the same frame.

There is a method for growing rhubarb called forcing. The plant is raised in total darkness, tended only in brief intervals of candlelight. It thrives by reaching toward an absent sun, stretching so fast its growth can be heard. Forcing can weaken the crop, but when done carefully, it yields something sweeter.

I am not making an allegory. I am just saying that some things grow toward what they cannot see, and the growing is not separate from the sweetness.

Perhaps love slips through our hands not because it is absent, but because we are not there. To love another person, a place, or life itself may mean remaining before it without retreat, allowing it to exist beyond our need to name it.
Nothing disappears all at once. Things remain with us long enough to become something else before we realize they have changed.

pages.title: After the
pages.note: Thus, understanding brings peace, but that peace is marked by the awareness that, in the end, there is no problem, and there never was.

pieces.text:
To understand the nature of existence is to realize that there is no problem to solve, only a continuous unfolding of what is.

As creatures shaped by the age and context in which we are born, we are often blind to the deeper truths of our reality.

Most live without ever questioning, caught in the flow of their time, while a few are driven to reflect on the fabric of life itself.

This reflection does not offer solutions, nor does it change the world around us, but it allows us to experience life in a more profound way, seeing beyond the surface.

The moment we realize that there is no inherent problem, no ultimate challenge that needs fixing, an understanding arises, and with it, a certain peace.

But this peace, paradoxically, is both liberating and empty.

Once we see that nothing holds ultimate meaning beyond its existence, we come face-to-face with the realization that everything just is, without reason or resolution.

This understanding neither gives us answers nor removes us from the cycle, it merely transforms our experience of it.
The search for meaning becomes an illusion in itself, but by raising ourselves beyond the noise, we witness the chaos with clarity, not seeking to escape it, but accepting it for what it is.
Thus, understanding brings peace, but that peace is marked by the awareness that, in the end, there is no problem, and there never was.

pages.title: More Sweet Than Bitter
paras: You know this the way you know weather. Not because someone explained it to you but because you stood inside it long enough. There are things that do not survive being named. You can circle them with language, you can build sentences that lean toward them the way trees lean toward light, but the thing itself stays where it is, untouched, whole, indifferent to your effort. This is not a failure of language. It is the shape of what is real.

We are prior to our words. Whatever we are, we were that before we learned to speak it, and whatever remains most true about us still lives there, in that silence before the first syllable. Every photograph, every poem, every careful arrangement of color and sound is an attempt to point back toward that place. Not to capture it. To confirm that it exists.

There is a method for growing rhubarb called forcing. The plant is raised in total darkness, tended only in brief intervals of candlelight. It thrives by reaching toward an absent sun, stretching so fast its growth can be heard. Forcing can weaken the crop, but when done carefully, it yields something sweeter. I am not making an allegory. I am just saying that some things grow toward what they cannot see, and the growing is not separate from the sweetness.

Sorrow does this. It moves through a place the way weather moves through a place, changing what it touches without destroying it. What remains after is not what was there before, but it is not nothing either. It is something else, something that has been through the full weight of what happened and did not empty out. You cannot explain this to someone who has not stood inside it. You can only show them, and hope they are willing to stay long enough to feel it.

The simplest things carry it. A gesture repeated so many times it has become invisible. A door that still opens. The way the light falls in a particular room at a particular hour as if it has been practicing for years. These are not symbols. They are not evidence of anything. They are just what is here, what keeps being here, ordinary and ordinary and ordinary until it breaks your heart.

There are moments when time slips and what was once returns to you so vividly, with such detail, that it unsettles you. Was it ever real, or only a dream? The question is not the point. The point is the returning, the fact that something in you still receives it, still trembles at it, still opens when every logic says to close. The fortunate ones are those who never lose this. Not innocence, not naivety, but the willingness to be astonished by what you have seen a thousand times, to feel that quiet tremor as if the world were revealing itself to you for the first time, again and again.
It's more sweet than bitter. You don't notice it at first. Then it doesn't leave.

pages.title: The Unfinished God
paras: He made it in six days. Not the slow, patient unfolding you might expect from something eternal, something with no appointments, no hunger, no fear of the dark, but six days, as if there were somewhere else to be on the seventh. This detail has always bothered me, though for years I couldn't say exactly why. The religious traditions I grew up around treated it as a given, a fact to be accepted or a metaphor to be explained away, but no one seemed troubled by the tempo of it. The urgency. The almost unseemly haste. You don't rush unless something is pressing on you. You don't count the days unless somewhere, underneath the making, there is impatience.
And then the harder question, the one that doesn't get asked at the dinner table or in the mosque or the church: for whom?

Before the first word of creation there was nothing. No witness. No ear pressed against the dark waiting for the light to be called into existence. No eye to watch the waters divide from the waters, the land rise from the sea, the animals arrive blinking into a world still wet with its own newness. The most absolute performance ever staged, and not a single seat filled. God, if the story is true, made the universe for an audience that did not yet exist, which means he made it for no one, which means the making itself was the point, which means something else entirely, something that theology has mostly preferred not to look at directly.

Because here is what that implies. It implies that at the origin of everything there is an unresolved longing. A need to be seen that preceded the existence of anything capable of seeing. You can dress it in the language of overflow, of divine goodness that cannot contain itself and must spill outward, and that is a beautiful thought, but it doesn't dissolve the strangeness. It just relocates it. A God who overflows is a God who was too full. Full of what? And why did that fullness need somewhere to go? These are not blasphemies. They are the questions the story generates if you take it seriously enough to follow it past the comfortable stopping points.

What I keep coming back to is this: he was showing off. The scale of it, the light, the firmament, the living creatures after their kind, the whole staggering inventory of existence, it has the quality of a gesture made toward someone. It has the texture of wanting to impress. But the only one present to be impressed was himself, and you cannot impress yourself without a kind of split, a division inside the self between the one performing and the one watching, and that division, that original fracture, may be the thing we have been living inside of ever since.

Look at the world right now. I mean look at it honestly, the way you look at something when you stop trying to make it mean something bearable. The wars that nobody wins but nobody stops. The ideologies that devour their own children. The absolute certainty on every side that their version of the light is the real one. The platforms built to be witnessed on, the endless performance of the self for an audience that is scrolling past, half-present, as absent in its own way as the void before creation. We live in a world of people showing off for no one, and we are exhausted by it, and we cannot stop, and I think this is not an accident. I think we inherited the condition.

If the maker was in a hurry, we have been running ever since. If the maker needed to be seen and had no one to see him, we have been performing ever since. If the world was built in six days by something that couldn't quite wait, then the cracks were always going to show. The chaos we are living in doesn't feel like a deviation from the original plan. It feels like the plan catching up with itself. It feels like what happens when you build fast and grand and don't stop to ask whether the foundation holds.

There is something almost tender in it, if you can hold it that way. The idea that even the first cause, the unmoved mover, the light before light, whatever you want to call the thing that started all of this, even that was not at peace. Even that was reaching toward something it couldn't name. And we are its image, as the story says, and the image is restless, and the image is performing, and the image is making and unmaking and making again, and resting on the seventh day only long enough to feel the ache of what it has done.

Six days. He was definitely in a hurry. And we have been paying for that hurry ever since, not as punishment, but as inheritance. The world is chaotic and unfinished and reaching toward a witness it cannot find because the very first act of making was exactly that: chaotic, rushed, magnificent, and aimed at an empty room.

pages.title: About
paras: Habib Saleh is a Lebanese visual artist working across photography, film, and writing. Rather than approaching these as separate disciplines, he sees them as different ways of following the same inquiry, each capable of expressing what the others cannot.

Working primarily in Lebanon, Saleh photographs the people and places closest to him — family, villages, cities, and the quiet rhythms of everyday life. Guided by natural light, long-term observation, and a sensitivity to the ordinary, his work explores presence, memory, time, and the fragile coexistence of beauty and devastation. Rather than centering extraordinary events, his photographs remain attentive to what continues around them: the gestures, relationships, and atmospheres through which life quietly persists.

Writing moves alongside the images as an equal part of his practice, not as explanation but as another way of approaching what cannot be fully held by a photograph. Together, photography, film, and text form an ongoing body of work that reflects on perception, the limits of language, and the experience of being alive.
To Pray Is to Wander About the Meaning of Life is the continuous body of work gathered here — a living manuscript that keeps unfolding. The printed book will one day emerge from it.
Habib Saleh also photographs on commission.
